passage:
The ability of certain fungi to decompose lignin — the tough, carbon-rich polymer that gives wood its structural rigidity — has long puzzled researchers. Lignin is among the most chemically stable organic compounds in nature, and its breakdown is essential to the global carbon cycle, yet until recently the biochemical mechanism underlying fungal lignin degradation remained poorly understood.

For decades, the leading hypothesis held that so-called white-rot fungi accomplished lignin degradation through a single class of enzymes known as laccases, copper-containing proteins that strip electrons from the lignin polymer in a process called oxidation. According to this hypothesis, laccase activity alone was sufficient to fragment lignin's complex ring-based structure into smaller molecules that could then be absorbed by the fungus. This account was appealing in its simplicity and appeared to be supported by the fact that white-rot fungi produce abundant laccases when grown on wood.

Subsequent research has shown, however, that the laccase-only account is incomplete. In a series of experiments conducted since the early 1990s, researchers discovered a second class of enzymes — peroxidases, which require hydrogen peroxide as a cofactor — that are produced by the same fungi and appear to be indispensable to lignin degradation. When peroxidase activity was chemically suppressed in laboratory cultures, lignin breakdown slowed dramatically even when laccase levels remained high, suggesting that the two enzyme classes function cooperatively rather than redundantly. A more plausible account now holds that laccases initiate the oxidation of lignin by removing electrons and destabilizing the polymer, while peroxidases complete the fragmentation by cleaving specific chemical bonds that laccases alone cannot break.

The cooperative model raises an important question about how fungi regulate the production of both enzyme classes in a coordinated fashion. Recent molecular studies suggest that the genes encoding peroxidases and laccases share regulatory sequences that respond to the same environmental signals — chiefly the concentration of available cellulose and the ambient nitrogen level. This finding is consistent with the cooperative model, since coordinated induction would ensure that neither enzyme is produced in excess of the other. Nonetheless, a key limitation remains: most of the supporting data comes from laboratory cultures of a handful of white-rot species, and it is not yet clear whether the same regulatory linkage operates in forest ecosystems, where fungal communities are far more complex and substrate conditions vary considerably. Whether the cooperative model holds in situ is therefore still an open question.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: White-rot fungi produce two classes of enzymes — laccases and peroxidases — that have been shown conclusively to operate cooperatively in all forest ecosystems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The discovery that peroxidases collaborate with laccases has replaced the earlier single-enzyme account of lignin degradation, though questions about how this system operates in natural settings remain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lignin's chemical stability makes it among the most difficult organic compounds for fungi to degrade, a fact that explains the central role of the global carbon cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Molecular studies have revealed that genes encoding laccases and peroxidases share regulatory sequences, resolving the long-standing puzzle of how white-rot fungi break down lignin.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cooperative model of lignin degradation is superior to the laccase-only hypothesis because laboratory experiments consistently support it across a wide range of white-rot species.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the move from the laccase-only hypothesis to the cooperative model (peroxidases + laccases) and closes by noting that field applicability is still uncertain — precisely what B captures.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage explicitly says the cooperative model has not been confirmed in forest ecosystems, so 'conclusively … in all forest ecosystems' is inaccurate.
explanations.B: Correct. Integrates both the evidentiary development and the remaining limitation.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of the opening background; this is motivation for the inquiry, not the main point.
explanations.D: Overstates the conclusion — the molecular-regulatory finding is described as 'consistent with' but not as 'resolving' the puzzle.
explanations.E: Misrepresents the scope of laboratory support; the passage says data comes from 'a handful of white-rot species,' not a wide range.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what distinguishes laccases from peroxidases in the cooperative model of lignin degradation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Laccases require hydrogen peroxide as a cofactor, while peroxidases function independently of any cofactor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laccases cleave the specific chemical bonds that peroxidases have destabilized.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laccases initiate oxidation by removing electrons from lignin, while peroxidases complete fragmentation by cleaving bonds laccases cannot break.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laccases are produced only at high cellulose concentrations, whereas peroxidases are induced by elevated nitrogen levels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Laccases are absent in forest ecosystems, while peroxidases have been documented in both laboratory and field settings.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'laccases initiate the oxidation of lignin by removing electrons and destabilizing the polymer, while peroxidases complete the fragmentation by cleaving specific chemical bonds that laccases alone cannot break.'
explanations.A: Reverses the cofactor relationship: it is peroxidases, not laccases, that require hydrogen peroxide.
explanations.B: Inverts the roles described in the passage; the passage gives cleavage to peroxidases, not laccases.
explanations.C: Correct. Direct paraphrase of the third paragraph's cooperative-model description.
explanations.D: The passage says both enzyme classes respond to the same signals (cellulose and nitrogen); it does not assign different signals to each.
explanations.E: No such claim is made in the passage; field presence of either enzyme class is left as an open question.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, prior to the research conducted since the early 1990s, scientists studying white-rot fungi would have been most likely to believe which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lignin degradation in fungi is driven primarily by peroxidases, with laccases playing only a minor supporting role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The global carbon cycle depends on multiple classes of fungal enzymes working in coordination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laccase production alone was sufficient to account for the breakdown of lignin in white-rot fungi.

choices.label: D
choices.text: White-rot fungi regulate enzyme production through sequences that respond to cellulose concentration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The chemical stability of lignin renders it resistant to enzymatic degradation by any known organism.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the laccase-only hypothesis as 'the leading hypothesis' for decades, explicitly stating that 'laccase activity alone was sufficient to fragment lignin's complex ring-based structure.'
explanations.A: This reverses the pre-1990s view; peroxidases were not part of the earlier account at all.
explanations.B: The coordinated multi-enzyme view is the new finding, not the pre-1990s consensus.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly inferred from the passage's characterization of the earlier laccase-only hypothesis.
explanations.D: The regulatory-sequence finding is recent molecular work, not a pre-1990s belief.
explanations.E: The passage says degradation was thought to occur through laccases, not that it was considered impossible.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the experiment in which peroxidase activity was chemically suppressed serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that laccases become more active when peroxidases are absent, compensating for the suppression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that peroxidases, not laccases, are the primary drivers of lignin degradation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide evidence that the two enzyme classes function cooperatively rather than either alone being sufficient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that hydrogen peroxide is toxic to the fungi when present in large quantities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why laboratory cultures of white-rot fungi cannot replicate field conditions.

explanations.correct: The author uses this experimental result — lignin breakdown slowed dramatically even when laccase levels remained high — to support the claim that the two enzyme classes work together, directly countering the laccase-only account.
explanations.A: The passage states laccase levels remained high but degradation still slowed; no compensatory increase is described.
explanations.B: The experiment shows peroxidases are necessary but does not frame them as the primary driver over laccases; the model is cooperative.
explanations.C: Correct. The function is to demonstrate cooperative necessity, supporting the cooperative model.
explanations.D: Hydrogen peroxide toxicity is never mentioned; this misrepresents the experimental design.
explanations.E: The passage raises the lab-vs.-field limitation separately in the final paragraph; this experiment is not about replicating field conditions.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the cooperative model of lignin degradation can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement tempered by awareness that the model has not yet been tested in any laboratory setting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious acceptance supported by experimental evidence, alongside acknowledgment of an unresolved limitation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: neutral presentation of a hypothesis that the author regards as no more convincing than the earlier laccase-only account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: skepticism about the model's validity because it has been derived exclusively from field studies rather than controlled experiments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: strong conviction that the cooperative model is definitively established and that remaining questions are of minor significance.

explanations.correct: The author calls the cooperative account 'more plausible,' cites supporting experimental evidence, and endorses the regulatory finding as 'consistent with' the model — but closes by flagging a 'key limitation' about field applicability. This maps to cautious acceptance with acknowledged uncertainty.
explanations.A: Overstates positivity and misstates the laboratory situation: most evidence is precisely from laboratory cultures, not absent from them.
explanations.B: Correct. Captures both the author's endorsement of the model and the explicit caveat about in situ verification.
explanations.C: The author clearly favors the cooperative model, calling it 'more plausible' — not neutral between the two accounts.
explanations.D: Inverts the data source: the limitation is that data comes only from lab settings, not only from the field.
explanations.E: Overstates certainty; the passage explicitly calls field applicability 'still an open question.'

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biological phenomenon is introduced; a competing pair of explanations is presented; one explanation is refuted; the passage concludes with a definitive resolution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A long-standing puzzle is introduced; the dominant hypothesis is described; new evidence motivates a revised model; the revised model's supporting molecular findings and remaining limitations are noted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An unsolved problem is stated; a series of failed hypotheses is catalogued; a currently favored hypothesis is presented without reservation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chemistry of lignin is explained in detail; laboratory methods for studying fungal enzymes are described; practical applications of the findings are proposed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A phenomenon is introduced; two independent explanations are shown to be equally valid; the passage argues for retaining the older explanation for practical reasons.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the puzzle; paragraph 2 presents the laccase-only hypothesis; paragraph 3 introduces new peroxidase evidence and the cooperative model; paragraph 4 discusses molecular regulatory support and field-applicability limitations. B matches this four-part arc exactly.
explanations.A: Misrepresents the ending: the passage does not reach a 'definitive resolution' but rather flags an open question.
explanations.B: Correct. Accurately maps all four paragraphs in sequence.
explanations.C: There is not a 'series of failed hypotheses'; only one prior hypothesis is discussed, and the new model is presented with reservations, not 'without reservation.'
explanations.D: The passage does not describe laboratory methods in detail, nor does it propose practical applications.
explanations.E: The two accounts are not treated as equally valid, and the passage does not argue for retaining the older explanation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the cooperative model is more plausible than the laccase-only hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Subsequent studies found that the chemical agent used to suppress peroxidase activity in the laboratory experiments also partially inhibited laccase function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: White-rot fungi that produce unusually high quantities of laccases tend to inhabit nitrogen-poor environments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The regulatory sequences shared by laccase and peroxidase genes were also found in fungi that do not degrade lignin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several white-rot species produce peroxidases only during the early stages of wood colonization and then cease production before lignin breakdown is complete.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Forest ecosystems harbor fungal species that degrade lignin at rates far slower than those observed in laboratory cultures.

explanations.correct: The cooperative model's key experimental support is that lignin breakdown slowed when peroxidases were suppressed even though laccases remained high. If the suppressing agent also partially inhibited laccases, the slowdown might be explained by reduced laccase activity, not by peroxidase necessity — thereby undermining the experiment's conclusion and the cooperative model's evidentiary basis.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly attacks the validity of the suppression experiment that underpins the cooperative model.
explanations.B: Laccase quantity varying with nitrogen levels is consistent with the regulatory picture and does not undermine the cooperative model.
explanations.C: Shared regulatory sequences in non-lignin-degrading fungi would complicate the regulatory story but not directly undermine the cooperative enzymatic model.
explanations.D: Early-stage-only peroxidase production might complicate the model, but the passage frames peroxidases as completing fragmentation — if lignin breakdown continues without them, this would weaken the model somewhat; however, A more directly undermines the specific experimental evidence the author cites.
explanations.E: Slower field rates relative to lab rates is consistent with the limitation the author already acknowledges and does not attack the cooperative model itself.

passage:
The origin of the Moon has been a source of sustained debate in planetary science. Early proposals ranged from the notion that the Moon was captured whole from an independent orbit to the idea that it spun off from a rapidly rotating proto-Earth. By the 1980s, however, a third proposal — the giant-impact hypothesis — had emerged as the consensus view, and it remains the framework within which most lunar research is conducted today.

The giant-impact hypothesis holds that, approximately 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body (commonly referred to as Theia) collided with the early Earth at an oblique angle. The collision vaporized much of Theia and a substantial portion of Earth's outer mantle, ejecting an enormous cloud of molten rock and gas into orbit. According to the hypothesis, this cloud eventually coalesced under gravity to form the Moon. Several lines of evidence appear to support this account. The Moon is notably deficient in iron relative to Earth, which is consistent with the idea that the ejected material came primarily from the silica-rich outer mantle rather than from the iron-rich cores of either body. Additionally, the Moon has a very small iron core of its own — a feature the hypothesis explains naturally. The ratio of stable oxygen isotopes in lunar and terrestrial rocks is nearly identical, suggesting that the two bodies share a common origin in the inner solar system.

In recent years, however, precise isotopic analyses have complicated this picture. Several elements besides oxygen — including tungsten, titanium, and chromium — show isotopic ratios in lunar rocks that are virtually indistinguishable from those of Earth's mantle. This degree of similarity is difficult to reconcile with a straightforward giant-impact scenario, because Theia, having formed elsewhere in the solar system, would almost certainly have had a distinct isotopic composition from Earth's. If the ejected cloud were a mixture of Theia material and Earth mantle material, the Moon should reflect that mixture — yet measurements suggest the Moon is nearly purely Earth-like in composition.

Researchers have proposed several modifications to address this inconsistency. One variant posits that Theia's composition happened to be nearly identical to Earth's, perhaps because both bodies accreted from material in similar regions of the solar nebula. Another variant suggests that the impact was far more energetic than originally modeled — creating a well-mixed, high-temperature disk in which material from Theia and Earth equilibrated before the Moon condensed, erasing any initial compositional difference. Neither variant has yet been definitively confirmed, and the question of how the Moon acquired such a strikingly Earth-like isotopic signature remains one of the more intriguing open problems in planetary science.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is most likely to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that the giant-impact hypothesis should be abandoned in favor of one of the two variant models described in the final paragraph.

choices.label: B
choices.text: describe the giant-impact hypothesis, explain why isotopic evidence has complicated it, and note that proposed modifications have not yet resolved the difficulty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: trace the complete history of scientific theories about the Moon's origin from the earliest proposals through the present day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that isotopic analysis is the most reliable method for determining the origin of bodies in the solar system.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that the Moon's iron deficiency and small core are the strongest pieces of evidence for a common origin with Earth.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the giant-impact hypothesis, presents its supporting evidence, then details the isotopic complication, and closes by noting that neither proposed modification has been confirmed — precisely the arc B describes.
explanations.A: The author does not advocate abandoning the giant-impact hypothesis; neither variant is endorsed as superior.
explanations.B: Correct. Captures the full rhetorical arc across all four paragraphs.
explanations.C: Too broad: the passage mentions earlier proposals only in passing and does not treat them as a 'complete history.'
explanations.D: Isotopic analysis is used as evidence, but the passage does not argue it is the most reliable method for solar-system body origins generally.
explanations.E: Too narrow: this characterizes only part of paragraph 2, not the passage as a whole.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Moon's relative deficiency in iron is consistent with the giant-impact hypothesis because

choices.label: A
choices.text: iron-poor bodies like Theia tend to form in the outer regions of the solar system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the Moon's iron core is thought to have been transferred from Earth's core during the impact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the material ejected into orbit came primarily from the silica-rich outer mantle rather than from the iron-rich cores of either body.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the impact generated temperatures high enough to vaporize most of the iron present in Earth's outer mantle.

choices.label: E
choices.text: iron settles toward the center of a planetary body during accretion, so lunar iron was never part of the ejected cloud.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the Moon's iron deficiency 'is consistent with the idea that the ejected material came primarily from the silica-rich outer mantle rather than from the iron-rich cores of either body.'
explanations.A: The passage says nothing about Theia being iron-poor or forming in the outer solar system.
explanations.B: No transfer of core material from Earth to Moon is described; the hypothesis focuses on ejected mantle material.
explanations.C: Correct. Close paraphrase of the passage's explicit statement.
explanations.D: The passage says the collision vaporized rock and gas but does not attribute the iron deficiency specifically to iron vaporization.
explanations.E: While iron settling during accretion is scientifically plausible, the passage does not offer this as its explanation for the Moon's iron deficiency.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, if Theia had formed in a region of the solar nebula with a distinctly different isotopic composition from Earth's, the giant-impact hypothesis in its original form would

choices.label: A
choices.text: predict that the Moon's isotopic ratios for elements such as tungsten and chromium would differ measurably from those of Earth's mantle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: require no modification, because the impact process naturally equalizes isotopic ratios between colliding bodies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: predict that the Moon would be compositionally similar to Earth because gravity selectively retains certain isotopes during coalescence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: be undermined by the oxygen-isotope similarity already established between lunar and terrestrial rocks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: be consistent with current measurements, which show that the Moon's composition is not purely Earth-like.

explanations.correct: The passage argues that if Theia had a distinct isotopic composition, the ejected cloud — a mixture of Theia and Earth material — should produce a Moon that reflects that mixture, differing from pure Earth-mantle composition. This is the very tension the recent isotopic data creates, and it follows logically that the original hypothesis would predict detectable isotopic differences.
explanations.A: Correct. Follows from the passage's reasoning that a mixed-origin disk should yield a Moon with a mixed (non-Earth-like) isotopic signature.
explanations.B: The passage offers natural equilibration only as one of the proposed variant modifications, not as an inherent property of the original hypothesis.
explanations.C: The passage does not describe gravity as selectively retaining isotopes during coalescence; this mechanism is not in the text.
explanations.D: The oxygen-isotope similarity is cited as supporting the original hypothesis, not as undermining it; the isotopic problem arises from the degree of similarity, not from a discrepancy.
explanations.E: Current measurements show the Moon IS nearly purely Earth-like, which is the problem for the original hypothesis, not evidence consistent with it.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of tungsten, titanium, and chromium in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide examples of elements whose isotopic ratios were used to confirm the capture hypothesis for the Moon's origin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that multiple independent isotopic analyses — not just oxygen — yield data that strain the original giant-impact model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that the Moon's mantle composition differs substantially from Earth's for most heavy elements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that isotopic analysis of lunar rocks is technically more accurate for heavy elements than for light ones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the isotopic compositions of lunar rocks with those of meteorites from the outer solar system.

explanations.correct: The author lists tungsten, titanium, and chromium alongside oxygen to show that the near-identical isotopic ratios between Moon and Earth extend across 'several elements,' reinforcing the point that this similarity is not an isolated anomaly but a broad pattern that challenges the original hypothesis.
explanations.A: These elements are presented as evidence complicating the giant-impact hypothesis, not as support for the capture hypothesis.
explanations.B: Correct. The function is to broaden the evidential challenge beyond oxygen to multiple elements.
explanations.C: The passage says the opposite: these ratios are 'virtually indistinguishable' from Earth's mantle — similarity, not difference.
explanations.D: No comparison of analytical accuracy between heavy and light elements is made in the passage.
explanations.E: No meteorites from the outer solar system are mentioned in this context.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which one of the following as one of the two variant modifications proposed to address the isotopic inconsistency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hypothesis that Theia was captured from the outer solar system, where bodies have lower metallic content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposal that the Moon formed from material ejected by multiple smaller impacts rather than a single giant one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The suggestion that Theia's composition was nearly identical to Earth's because both accreted from material in similar regions of the solar nebula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The argument that early lunar volcanism redistributed isotopic ratios over billions of years, producing an artificially Earth-like signature.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The claim that stable oxygen isotopes do not vary across the inner solar system and therefore cannot serve as compositional markers.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that 'one variant posits that Theia's composition happened to be nearly identical to Earth's, perhaps because both bodies accreted from material in similar regions of the solar nebula.'
explanations.A: Theia being captured from the outer solar system is not mentioned as a proposed variant; the passage says Theia 'formed elsewhere in the solar system' without specifying capture.
explanations.B: Multiple smaller impacts are not discussed anywhere in the passage.
explanations.C: Correct. Direct paraphrase of the first variant described in the final paragraph.
explanations.D: Lunar volcanism redistributing isotopes is not mentioned in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage cites oxygen-isotope similarity as evidence supporting the hypothesis, not as a methodological flaw.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the giant-impact hypothesis can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unconditional acceptance, given that three independent lines of evidence from paragraph two have collectively confirmed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissal, on the grounds that recent isotopic data have proven the hypothesis incompatible with observed lunar composition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: measured support for the hypothesis as a framework while acknowledging that recent isotopic findings pose a genuine, unresolved challenge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the author regards the question of the Moon's origin as peripheral to the central concerns of planetary science.

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarded preference for one of the variant models over the original hypothesis, though the author stops short of endorsing it explicitly.

explanations.correct: The author treats the giant-impact hypothesis as 'the consensus view' within which 'most lunar research is conducted,' and presents supporting evidence approvingly — yet devotes the final two paragraphs to a genuine complication and notes that neither proposed fix has been 'definitively confirmed.' This is measured support with acknowledged difficulty.
explanations.A: Overstates certainty; the passage flags a significant unresolved complication and does not treat the hypothesis as confirmed.
explanations.B: The author does not characterize the hypothesis as disproven or incompatible; the complications are real but the hypothesis remains the dominant framework.
explanations.C: Correct. Accurately captures the author's balanced stance.
explanations.D: The author calls the open question 'one of the more intriguing open problems in planetary science,' indicating engagement, not indifference.
explanations.E: The author presents both variants without preferring either; no guarded preference for one variant is expressed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following hypothetical findings would most closely parallel the role that the recent multi-element isotopic data play in the passage's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A study confirms that the Moon's iron core is slightly larger than previously estimated, strengthening the giant-impact hypothesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: New measurements reveal that Mars's two small moons share an isotopic signature nearly identical to that of asteroids in the outer belt, complicating the hypothesis that they were captured from that region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory simulations show that silica-rich material can be ejected from a planetary mantle at lower impact velocities than previously thought.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Astronomers detect a Mars-sized body currently orbiting the Sun, suggesting that bodies similar to Theia still exist in the solar system.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers find that white-rot fungi degrade lignin faster in nitrogen-poor soils, supporting the cooperative enzyme model.

explanations.correct: In the passage, multi-element isotopic data that are more similar than expected between Moon and Earth complicate a widely accepted origin hypothesis by revealing a match that the hypothesis cannot easily explain. Choice B presents an analogous situation: isotopic similarity between Mars's moons and outer-belt asteroids complicates the very hypothesis (capture from that region) those moons were supposed to support, because captured bodies should share the signature of their source — but if the similarity is unexpectedly high in a way that doesn't fit, it creates the same kind of puzzle.
explanations.A: This strengthens rather than complicates a hypothesis; the parallel role in the passage is to complicate an accepted account.
explanations.B: Correct. Isotopic data unexpectedly similar to a source region complicates an accepted capture hypothesis — the same logical structure as the passage's isotopic challenge to the giant-impact model.
explanations.C: This refines a parameter within the existing model rather than posing a challenge that requires new variants, unlike the role of the isotopic data.
explanations.D: Detecting a surviving Theia-like body might be interesting but does not parallel the role of evidence that challenges the existing hypothesis.
explanations.E: This belongs to the other passage's subject matter and does not parallel the role of complicating evidence for an established planetary-science hypothesis.
